name: Briddim
tagline: Homestay village above the old trade road to Tibet
meta_description: Briddim, a Tibetan-Tamang homestay village at 2,230 m above Syabrubesi: community homestays, the gompa, the Kerung trade route and the Tamang Heritage Trail.
summary: Briddim is a Buddhist village of Tamang and Tibetan heritage at about 2,230 m on the hillside north of Syabrubesi. It is known for its community homestays, its gompa and its view over the Bhote Koshi valley, the old trade route to Kerung in Tibet. It closes the Tamang Heritage Trail loop.
intro: Briddim lies on a sunny shelf of farmland at about 2,230 m, high above the Bhote Koshi between Syabrubesi and Timure. Its stone houses, prayer flags and small gompa look across the valley to the ridges of the Langtang range. It is a village of Buddhist families who call themselves Tamang and trace much of their culture to Tibet, a few days' walk to the north along the old Kerung road.

For travellers, Briddim is best known for its community homestays. Instead of lodges, guests stay with families who take turns hosting through a village committee, eat at their hearth and share the rhythm of a farming day. It is usually the last night of the Tamang Heritage Trail before Syabrubesi, and also a quieter alternative to sleeping in Syabrubesi before or after the Langtang trek.

The village stands well above the river that flooded on 26 August 2026, but the valley below, including Timure and Syabrubesi, was devastated and road access was cut. Many Briddim families have relatives who worked on the border road or in Syabrubesi. Check current status before you travel; when access reopens, a homestay night here is one of the most useful ways to support the area.

story.title: A village looking down on the road to Kerung
paras: The Bhote Koshi valley below Briddim was for centuries a trade road between Kathmandu and the Tibetan town of Kerung, now Gyirong. Caravans of salt, wool and grain passed through Timure and over the border at Rasuwagadhi. Villages on the slopes above, like Briddim, supplied porters, pack animals and food, and their families married and traded across the border. Language, dress and religion in Briddim still show those ties. Older people in Briddim still remember when the valley road was a footpath and when trips to Kerung took several days of walking with loads on the back. Their stories are the best guide to how the valley used to work.

The route had its wars as well as its markets. In 1792 Qing Chinese troops came down this valley toward Nuwakot, and in 1855 Nepal built the fort at Rasuwagadhi during its war with Tibet. In the 20th century the border closed and reopened with politics. In 2014 Rasuwagadhi became an international trade crossing, and trucks returned to the valley road below the village, now motor road rather than mule track. Each change brought new work for people in Briddim, as porters, drivers, traders and labourers, and each closure took some of that work away. The village learned to adapt to whatever the border and the road brought.

Briddim chose a different path to an income: community tourism. Families opened their homes to visitors as part of the Tamang Heritage Trail, sharing guests through a village committee so that the money spread across households. The 2015 earthquake damaged houses and the gompa, and the village rebuilt. The floods of 2025 and 2026 destroyed the border road and much of Syabrubesi; Briddim, on its high shelf, now waits for the road and the visitors to return. When it does, the homestays will be waiting, and so will the people who run them.

people: Briddim's families are Buddhist Tamang with strong Tibetan heritage; People speak Tamang, Tibetan dialects and Nepali. They farm potatoes, maize, barley and buckwheat, keep cattle and yak crossbreeds, run homestays, and work in Syabrubesi, Kathmandu or abroad. Elders often speak little Nepali, while children learn it at school.

untold.fact: The Rasuwagadhi crossing below Briddim opened to international trade in December 2014, after Nepal and China agreed in 2012 to develop it, and became an alternative to the Kodari crossing.
In Gyirong town across the border, the old Kerung of Nepali traders, live the Daman people, descendants of Nepali Gorkha soldiers from centuries ago, who were granted Chinese citizenship in 2003.
A flood on 8 July 2025, a year before the larger 2026 disaster, destroyed the Miteri Bridge at Rasuwagadhi and washed away around 1 km of the road between Timure and the border.

taste.name: Tibetan bread and butter tea
taste.text: Breakfast in a Briddim homestay often means Tibetan bread, a puffy fried dough, with honey or jam, and salty butter tea or sweet milk tea. Dinners are dal bhat, potatoes or thukpa. Ask your host for tsampa, roasted barley flour, which older people still eat daily.

facts: ≈ 120 km to Syabrubesi + 3–4 h walk or a short jeep ride
Community homestays, gompa, Tamang Heritage Trail

highlights.title: Community homestays
highlights.text: Families take turns hosting guests through a village committee, so income spreads across Briddim. You eat at the family hearth, sleep in a simple room and share the household's day. It is a slower, more personal night than any lodge in Syabrubesi could offer.

highlights.title: The village gompa
highlights.text: Briddim's small monastery, repaired after 2015, is the centre of village ritual life. Visit with your host in the morning, spin the prayer wheels clockwise and leave a small offering. Older villagers often circle it at dawn and dusk, turning the wheels as they walk.

highlights.title: View over the Bhote Koshi
highlights.text: From the edge of the village you look down on the valley of the old Kerung trade road and across to the snow ridges of the Langtang range, especially clear in autumn and winter mornings.

highlights.title: End of the Heritage Trail
highlights.text: Briddim is usually the last night on the Tamang Heritage Trail, reached from Thuman or Timure, before the walk down to Syabrubesi. It is a calm place to finish a trek. Many trekkers say it is their favourite night of the whole loop.

highlights.title: Farm life
highlights.text: Fields of potatoes, buckwheat and barley surround the village. Join your hosts in the fields, watch grain being dried and ground, and see how a mountain household feeds itself. Ask your guide to translate as your hosts explain the farming calendar.

how_to_reach.text: From Syabrubesi, walk up about 3 to 4 hours on a steady trail through forest and farmland. From Thuman or Timure on the Tamang Heritage Trail, a day's walk.
A rough road links Briddim with the valley below. The roads around Syabrubesi and Timure were badly damaged in the 26 August 2026 flood; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Briddim has no hotels; guests stay in community homestays in family houses, arranged through the village homestay committee, which shares guests among member households. Rooms are simple and clean, with blankets or quilts, shared toilets and home-cooked meals. Hot water is limited. We confirm availability with the committee before you travel, since the post-flood period has disrupted visitors and supplies. Tell us about dietary needs early so hosts can plan meals.
tips: Accept the homestay your committee assigns; the rotation is how the village shares income fairly.
Bring a small gift such as fruit, biscuits or notebooks for the children of your host family.
Pass chortens and mani walls keeping them on your right.
Pack a warm sleeping bag for winter nights, which drop near freezing.
Check road and trail status around Syabrubesi before you travel, as the 2026 flood changed access.

experiences.title: Community homestay night in Briddim
experiences.summary: Stay with a Buddhist Tamang family in Briddim through the village's community homestay system, eat at the hearth, visit the gompa and wake to views of the Langtang range. It is the village's own way of welcoming guests.
body: When you arrive, the homestay committee assigns you to a family whose turn it is to host. This rotation is a point of pride in Briddim: it spreads the income fairly across the village. Your hosts welcome you with tea, often with a khata scarf, and show you to a simple room in their stone house. The committee also sets the price, so every family charges the same rate. Do not ask to change houses unless there is a real problem; your guide will handle it quietly if needed.

Evenings are spent in the kitchen, the warmest room. Meals might be dal bhat, potatoes with chilli pickle, thukpa or Tibetan bread, and your hosts may offer butter tea or chhyang. Your guide helps with conversation about farming, family, religion, and life in the valley since the floods. Expect to eat with your fingers or a spoon, sitting on low stools or cushions around the fire. Try a little of everything you are offered, and say clearly if you have had enough, since hosts will keep refilling your plate otherwise.

In the morning, walk to the gompa with your host, help in the fields if work is under way, and watch the sun come up over the ridges. The homestay fee is paid through the committee to the household, and your visit directly supports families in an area hit hard by the 2026 disaster. Before you leave, thank your hosts by name and, if you wish, give a small gift for the household. A white khata scarf, offered with both hands, is a respected way to say goodbye in this Buddhist village.

faqs.q: How do Briddim's homestays work?
faqs.a: A village committee manages the homestays and assigns guests to member families in rotation, so that income is shared across households. You pay a set rate that includes dinner and breakfast. Rooms are simple, toilets are shared and meals are eaten with the family. We book through the committee in advance.

faqs.q: Is Briddim good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. Children usually enjoy farm animals, village children and the slower pace. Facilities are basic, nights can be cold and the walk up from Syabrubesi takes 3 to 4 hours, so plan for that. In the post-flood period, check current status of road access before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stay in Briddim before the Langtang trek?
faqs.a: Yes. When access allows, a night in Briddim before or after the Langtang Valley trek is a calmer alternative to Syabrubesi. Upper trails also link Briddim with the Langtang route via Khanjim and Sherpagaon. Your guide will plan the best connection based on current trail conditions.

experiences.title: Morning at the Briddim gompa
experiences.summary: Join villagers at the small gompa in the early morning as butter lamps are lit, prayer wheels turn and older residents walk their circuits, with your host explaining the images and rituals. It is a calm start to the day.
body: Briddim's gompa sits among the houses, with prayer wheels set into its walls and flags strung above. It was damaged in the 2015 earthquake and repaired by the village. In the early morning, older residents walk around it clockwise, spinning the wheels and murmuring mantras. Join them for a circuit or two if you like: walk slowly, clockwise, and turn the wheels with your right hand. Nobody minds visitors taking part, as long as you follow the direction and keep the pace of the people in front of you.

If the caretaker or lama is present, you may be invited inside. Take off your shoes and hat, walk clockwise, and sit quietly while lamps are lit. Images usually include Guru Padmasambhava and the Buddha, along with protector deities. Ask before photographing inside. Inside, the light is dim and the air smells of butter lamps and incense. Sit cross-legged on the floor or on a cushion near the back, keep your feet tucked under you, and stay quiet. If a lama is chanting, wait until he pauses before you get up to leave.

Your host or guide can explain the gompa's role in village life: blessings for new houses and fields, funerals, festivals such as Sonam Lhosar and Buddha Jayanti. Leave a small donation for the butter lamps before you go. The gompa depends on village contributions for lamps, repairs and festival costs, and visitors' donations help. Put money in the box near the door or hand it to the caretaker with both hands. Your guide can tell you what is usual.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit the gompa in Briddim?
faqs.a: Yes, when the caretaker or lama is there and the door is open. Go with your host or guide, take off shoes and hat, walk clockwise and keep quiet. Do not touch statues or offerings, and ask before photographing. A small donation is appreciated.

faqs.q: What should I wear to visit a gompa?
faqs.a: Modest clothes covering shoulders and knees, and shoes you can slip off easily. Remove your hat inside. In winter, bring warm socks, as gompa floors are cold. Avoid pointing your feet toward the altar when sitting. Long trousers or a long skirt are best.

faqs.q: What are prayer wheels for?
faqs.a: Prayer wheels contain rolled paper printed with mantras, most often Om mani padme hum. Turning a wheel clockwise is believed to send the prayers out as if they had been recited. Villagers spin them while walking around the gompa every morning and evening.

experiences.title: Farm day with a Briddim family
experiences.summary: Spend a morning in the fields with your host family, depending on the season planting or harvesting potatoes, cutting buckwheat or barley, and learn how the harvest becomes the dishes you eat at dinner. Every season brings different work.
body: Farming in Briddim follows the seasons. In spring, potatoes are planted and fields prepared; in autumn, potatoes are dug, buckwheat and barley harvested and grain dried on flat roofs and courtyards. Work is done mostly by hand, with tools that have changed little in generations. Families share labour at busy times, working on each other's fields in turn, so you may find several households working together. It is social work, with tea breaks, jokes and songs, and visitors are welcomed into it.

With your host, you walk to their fields at the edge of the village and join in for a couple of hours. Your guide translates as they explain which crops grow at what height, how they store food for winter and how the market for potatoes has changed with the road and, now, its loss. Potatoes from Briddim and nearby villages used to be sold in Syabrubesi and Kathmandu. With the road cut in 2026, families face the problem of getting crops to market, and many will talk openly about it.

Back in the kitchen, you help prepare lunch from what you have picked: boiled potatoes with chilli and salt, buckwheat pancakes or a simple curry. It is not a show; it is ordinary work that keeps the village fed. Afterwards, wash at the outdoor tap and rest in the sun. Most people find a few hours of field work at 2,230 m tiring, which tells you something about the strength of the people who do it every day. Hosts appreciate the help, however clumsy.

faqs.q: Do I need to be fit to join a farm day?
faqs.a: No special fitness is needed, but field work involves bending, carrying and walking on uneven terraces, often in the sun. Work at your own pace and stop when you want. Bring a hat, sunscreen, gloves if you have them, and clothes that can get dirty.

faqs.q: What crops grow in Briddim?
faqs.a: Potatoes are the main crop, along with maize, barley, buckwheat and some vegetables. Many families also keep cattle and yak crossbreeds for milk, butter and manure. Crop choice depends on altitude and season, and the rhythm of planting and harvest shapes the village year.

faqs.q: Is a farm day available all year?
faqs.a: Farm work happens through much of the year, but the most interesting times are spring planting from March to May and the autumn harvest from September to November. In winter there is less field work, and in the monsoon heavy rain makes some days unsuitable.

experiences.title: Walk down from Briddim to Syabrubesi
experiences.summary: The closing walk of the Tamang Heritage Trail, descending through forest and farmland from Briddim to Syabrubesi, with views over the Bhote Koshi valley and the Langtang Khola confluence. Allow a relaxed morning for it.
body: Leaving Briddim after breakfast, the trail drops through terraced fields and then through oak and rhododendron forest, with occasional views down to the Bhote Koshi and across to the hills of the Langtang Valley. It is a steady descent of about 750 m that takes around 3 hours. The path is clear but steep in places, and the forest sections can be slippery after rain. Use poles, take your time and let faster walkers pass. Your guide will stop at a viewpoint where the whole valley opens up below.

Along the way you pass small chortens and prayer flags, and maybe herders bringing animals up or down. Your guide points out the line of the old trade road along the valley floor and the places where the 2025 and 2026 floods changed the river. It is a good moment to ask about the trade road and the border, since many families in Briddim worked there. Ask gently, as many people lost friends and relatives in the 2026 flood, and let your guide judge what is appropriate to discuss.

Below, Syabrubesi itself is rebuilding after the August 2026 flood. Depending on conditions, we may arrange onward transport from a different point; check current status before you travel. The walk is a fitting close to a trek through Tamang country. If you are continuing to the Langtang Valley, the trail up the Langtang Khola begins from the Syabrubesi side. If you are heading home, your guide will confirm the current road route to Kathmandu before you leave Briddim, since conditions change week to week.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Briddim to Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: About 3 hours downhill, descending around 750 m through farmland and forest. Going up takes 3 to 4 hours. Use walking poles to save your knees, and take care on loose or wet sections. Start in the morning to reach the valley before the afternoon heat.

faqs.q: Is the Briddim trail safe after the 2026 flood?
faqs.a: Briddim and the upper trail lie well above the Bhote Koshi, but the valley floor and Syabrubesi were badly damaged on 26 August 2026, and riverbanks may be unstable. Your guide will choose the route based on current local advice. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do Briddim as a side trip from Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Yes. When access is open, walk up to Briddim in 3 to 4 hours, spend a night in a homestay and come down next morning. It makes a good extra day before or after the Langtang Valley trek, and helps acclimatisation by climbing to 2,230 m before going higher.

faqs.q: Where is Briddim?
faqs.a: Briddim is a village in Rasuwa district, Bagmati Province, at about 2,230 m on the hillside north of Syabrubesi, above the Bhote Koshi valley between Syabrubesi and Timure. It is 3 to 4 hours' walk from Syabrubesi and is part of the Tamang Heritage Trail.

faqs.q: What is Briddim known for?
faqs.a: Its community homestays, run through a village committee that rotates guests among families, its Buddhist gompa, and its strong Tamang and Tibetan culture. It also has wide views over the Bhote Koshi valley, the old trade route to Kerung in Tibet, and toward the Langtang range.

faqs.q: How do I get to Briddim?
faqs.a: Usually on foot from Syabrubesi in 3 to 4 hours, or from Thuman or Timure on the Tamang Heritage Trail. A rough road also reaches the village. Roads in the valley below were badly damaged in the 26 August 2026 flood; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Was Briddim affected by the August 2026 flood?
faqs.a: The village itself sits high above the river and was not in the flood's path, but the valley below, including Timure and Syabrubesi, was devastated, and many Briddim families lost relatives, jobs or property there. Road access was cut. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Briddim on the Tamang Heritage Trail?
faqs.a: Yes. Briddim is usually the last night of the 5 to 7 day Tamang Heritage Trail loop, after Gatlang, Tatopani, Nagthali, Thuman and Timure, before the descent to Syabrubesi. Some trekkers also add it before or after the Langtang Valley trek.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Briddim?
faqs.a: Briddim lies in the Langtang National Park area, and foreign trekkers need the park permit. Since April 2023, foreign trekkers in national parks must go with a licensed guide. Additional controls may apply in the post-flood period. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Briddim?
faqs.a: October to December for clear skies and the harvest, and March to April for spring planting and warmer days. Winter is cold but often clear and quiet. Avoid June to September, when monsoon rain makes trails slippery and roads unreliable.

faqs.q: What language do people speak in Briddim?
faqs.a: Tamang and Tibetan dialects at home and Nepali with outsiders. Many younger people speak some English. Greet people with Tashi delek or the Tamang Fyafulla. A guide who speaks Nepali and ideally Tamang will help you get much more from conversations with your hosts.

faqs.q: How long should I stay in Briddim?
faqs.a: One night is the minimum and fits most Tamang Heritage Trail itineraries. Two nights let you join a farm day, visit the gompa at a slow pace and walk to viewpoints around the village. When the area reopens after the 2026 flood, extra nights also bring needed income.
